title: Lyra Systems tokenflow workshop
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
summary: Discovery/workshop to map Lyra's expected tokenflow and p95 SLOs for a streaming chat/summary product. Discussed burst patterns, steady-state token/sec, first-token p95 goals, routing (hosted/dedicated/private), and compliance gating (EU data residency, KMS). Agreed to run an instrumented benchmark with sample prompts and to share security pack and pricing tiers.
header:
Date: 2026-04-18 16:00 UTC
Duration: 57 minutes
Attendees: Morgan, Priya, Diego (Redwood) — Tom, Nina, Sam, Ayesha (Lyra Systems)
Recording: Yes
Meeting type: Discovery / workshop
transcript:
00:00:00 Morgan (Redwood): Hey everybody thanks for hopping on, uh I'm Morgan from Redwood, I'm the AE working with Lyra. How's everyone doing?
00:00:05 Tom (Lyra): Good thanks Morgan, Tom here, CTO. We've got Nina, Sam, and Ayesha on the line.
00:00:12 Morgan: Awesome, quick intro from Priya and Diego — Priya leads infra perf at Redwood, Diego is our solutions eng who'll run the bench with you.
00:00:20 Priya (Redwood): Hi all, excited to dig in. We'll try to keep it focused on the p95 and token flow numbers you shared in the survey.
00:00:27 Sam (Lyra): Great — we sent the traffic shape doc; main thing: 3K DAUs at launch, but really worried about spikes. We expect steady-state about 150 qps and bursts to 1,200 qps for short periods (30s-4m).
00:00:40 Priya: Ok that's helpful. When you say 150 qps that's requests per second — what is the average token output per request?
00:00:46 Sam: Average ~120 tokens, but some summary responses are 400-600 tokens. Some analytics flows will stream back long transcripts, up to 2k tokens.
00:00:55 Diego (Redwood): So to translate — steady-state tokens/sec is ~18k tokens/sec (150 * 120), and burst could be ~240k tokens/sec (1,200 * 200 avg during burst) if those bursts contain larger responses. There's lots of nuance but that's the back-of-envelope.
00:01:10 Nina (Lyra): We're aiming for an end-user p95 of first-streamed-token under 300ms for chat and a steady-state p95 per token under 40ms. Is that realistic on hosted?
00:01:20 Priya: Good question. For hosted we've seen first-token p95s in the 200-350ms range for mid-size open models on optimized instances. Steady-state per-token times around 15-40ms depending on model, kv-cache warm state, quantization, and sequence length.
00:01:35 Ayesha (Lyra): From security — we need EU data residency, SOC 2, and KMS integration for customer keys. Also SSO via SAML and RBAC. Can hosted satisfy that or do we need private?
00:01:46 Morgan: Hosted can satisfy SOC 2, SAML SSO, and we have KMS integrations for dedicated/private customers. For EU residency we have region selection on hosted, but if you need a private control plane and on-prem encryption keys, that's where Redwood Private comes in. There are trade-offs — we'll outline.
00:02:00 Tom: Great. For capacity planning: what bucket would you put us in for an initial dedicated pool? We want predictable p95 under load.
:02:06 Priya: If your steady-state is 18k tokens/sec, that maps to roughly a 2-4 GPU dedicated pool depending on model size/quantization and whether you use batching and our KV cache. For burst handling to 240k tokens/sec you'd want a burst policy with queued capacity or autoscale; we often recommend a mixed approach: dedicated steady pool + reserved burst headroom or cross-region fallback.
00:02:25 Sam: Can you explain the KV cache effect? We have lots of short chats, so warm cache matters.
00:02:30 Priya: Sure — when KV cache is warm, generation for repeated or multi-turn chats avoids recomputing the full prefix. That lowers steady-state per-token cost and latency. Cold starts (first token) are dominated by model load and routing overhead. We also do prefix caching and continuous batching optimizations.
00:02:45 Diego: Also quantization matters: an 8-bit quantized variant can reduce GPU memory footprint and increase throughput; but sometimes p95 tail increases slightly depending on kernel selection. We'll show you model-level profiles in the bench.
00:02:58 Nina: Are there any streaming-specific SLOs we should model? Like p95 for first token vs per-token steady-state vs end-to-end time for 500 token response?
00:03:06 Priya: Yes we separate into three metrics: first-byte p95, steady-state per-token p95, and tail latency for full response completion p95. If you care about interactive feel, first-byte and per-token are primary. For 500 tokens with per-token 30ms p95 you're looking at ~15s for the streamed content (plus jitter).
00:03:20 Sam: 15s is fine for long summaries but we need the UI to show progressive streaming within 500ms for first chunk or the UX suffers.
00:03:27 Morgan: Note that first-chunk heuristics in the client can show partial tokens while backend continues generation; that helps UX.
00:03:32 Ayesha: From security/acceptance, we need audit logs for each request, and retention configurable to 365 days. Do you provide that in hosted?
00:03:41 Morgan: Audit logs and per-request metadata are available; retention and export to your SIEM are available as add-ons or standard on Dedicated/Private. We'll include details in the security pack we share.
00:03:52 Tom: For benchmarking — what's a typical benchmarking session look like? We want to replicate our traffic shape and evaluate p95 under canonical prompts.
00:03:59 Diego: We'll run instrumented runs with your prompts, mix short/medium/long responses, include cold-starts and steady-state. We'll capture first-token p95, per-token steady p95, throughput (tokens/sec), and GPU utilization. We'll also test dedicated pools and a hosted baseline.
00:04:12 Sam: How long does that take?
00:04:14 Diego: Usually 2-4 hours to set up and run several scenarios; we'll schedule a run window so we can triage and iterate.
00:04:20 Priya: For your burst profile specifically, we'll run a 5-minute ramp to peak and a 15-minute sustained test. That should reveal autoscale and queuing behavior.
00:04:29 Nina: Any gotchas with quantized variants for streaming? We've heard that quantization can change per-token pacing.
00:04:34 Priya: True — quantization reduces throughput variance but sometimes shifts tail if kernel selection isn't ideal. We'll test both float16 and q4/q8 variants. Also network egress and routing can add 20-40ms depending on region.
00:04:45 Ayesha: Do you have examples of cost comparisons? We need a rough delta between hosted per-token pricing and typical Dedicated committed capacity estimate.
00:04:52 Morgan: We'll send a cost model after the bench: per-token hosted estimate and committed Dedicated monthly estimate given your steady-state. Usually Dedicated reduces unit cost 20-50% depending on utilization.
00:05:00 Tom: Ok great. A little detail — our traffic is heavily EU in weeknights and US mornings; we want cross-region failover with minimal added latency. How does Redwood handle fallback?
00:05:09 Priya: Smart routing plus region failover. We can route by policy and warm small standby pools in a nearby region; fallback can add 50-150ms depending on distance and coldness of cache. For strict SLOs you can pin traffic to a region and use multi-region only for emergency fallbacks.
00:05:22 Sam: Any mention of burst queuing thresholds and token backlog? If requests exceed GPU capacity what happens?
00:05:28 Diego: We support configurable queueing and shedding. For user-facing chat we recommend queuing with soft-failover to a lighter model variant to preserve UX. We can also return progress updates for long running responses.
00:05:37 Nina: For the bench we need to supply sample prompts and redwood-runner config?
00:05:41 Diego: Yes — we'll give you a runner template and a prompts corpus. Ideally you provide realistic distribution: short/medium/long and a few worst-case long transcripts.
00:05:50 Ayesha: Quick question — does Redwood store customer data on managed hosted and how is it encrypted at rest?
00:05:55 Morgan: By default hosted stores used for service health and telemetry; you can opt-out of retention. Encryption at rest is AES-256; for customer-managed keys we support KMS integrations in Dedicated and Private. We'll include details in SOC 2 pack.
00:06:05 Tom: Ok any rough numbers for per-GPU tokens/sec for models akin to the ones we plan to use?
00:06:10 Priya: Rough ballpark: on an A100-style SKU a mid-sized model at fp16 can sustained 30-60k tokens/sec per GPU in steady-state with good batching. With q4/q8 that can be 60-120k tokens/sec. These vary by sequence length and kernel choices. We'll show GPU-side throughput traces in the bench.
00:06:25 Sam: That maps — if we need 18k tokens/sec steady-state, one GPU might suffice depending on batching and warm cache, but we want headroom and p95 consistency so 2 GPUs for steady-state plus burst policy seems safer.
00:06:35 Priya: Agreed.
00:06:36 Tom: What's the expected p95 first-token when routing to dedicated within same region?
00:06:40 Priya: Typically 120-260ms for first-byte on dedicated if instance is warm and KV cache warm; for cold model loads it can be seconds. So we focus on keeping warm pools for interactivity-sensitive endpoints.
00:06:52 Ayesha: Is there an SLA for p95 or uptime for Dedicated?
00:06:55 Morgan: We offer SLA for availability and best-effort latency targets on Dedicated. Specific p95 latency SLAs can be negotiated in enterprise contracts. We'll flag that with sales ops.
00:07:03 Sam: We asked about function/tool calling and whether tokenization overhead affects p95 — do you have guidance?
00:07:09 Priya: Function/tool calling adds a bit of extra round trips depending on your orchestration. We recommend batching tool calls and using local pre/post processing to minimize extra tokens. Tokenization overhead is usually small compared to generation time but does show up in microbenchmarks.
00:07:22 Tom: Anything else on our side you need before the bench?
00:07:24 Diego: Runner access, prompts, and a realistic traffic distribution. Also a list of models you want tested and whether to include quantized variants.
00:07:30 Nina: We'll provide that by Tuesday.
00:07:33 Morgan: Cool. Let's do a quick recap and next steps.
00:07:35 Morgan: Recap: Redwood will run an instrumented benchmark covering first-token p95, steady per-token p95, full-response tail, and tokens/sec across hosted baseline and a Dedicated pool. We'll test float16 and q variants, simulate your burst profile, and produce a report with GPU traces and cost estimates.
00:07:50 Tom: And security pack and SOC2 docs?
00:07:52 Morgan: Yes, security pack, SOC2 summary, and KMS/SSO integration docs will be shared.
00:07:57 Ayesha: One last nit: please include an SSO SAML flow diagram and example SAML metadata exchange.
00:08:03 Diego: We'll include that.
00:08:05 Priya: Any preference for a follow-up slot for the bench results?
00:08:08 Tom: Next Thursday same time if possible.
00:08:11 Morgan: I'll book provisional time. Thanks everyone.
00:08:14 Sam: Thanks.
00:08:16 End of meeting

Notes: Transcript has occasional mis-attributions and auto-captions errors (e.g., 'K V cash' for 'KV cache').
